claims.text: Precisely controlled, balanced precursor atomic ratios increase configurational mixing entropy during synthesis.
Increasing mixing entropy promotes formation of a homogeneous single-phase noble metal–based high-entropy alloy.
Increased configurational entropy minimizes elemental segregation.
Reduced elemental segregation produces a uniform atomic distribution.
A homogeneous single-phase structure stabilizes catalytic active sites.
A homogeneous single-phase structure increases the exposure of catalytic active sites.
Greater active-site stability and exposure support faster reaction kinetics.
Balanced precursor ratios will predominantly produce homogeneous single-phase nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles made with balanced precursor ratios will have higher catalytic rates than nanoparticles made with off-stoichiometric ratios.
Off-stoichiometric precursor ratios encourage phase segregation.
High-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized without strict precursor-ratio control typically exhibit partial phase segregation.
Partially phase-segregated nanoparticles typically have lower catalytic performance than homogeneous single-phase nanoparticles.
High-resolution TEM can assess the degree of alloy homogeneity versus phase segregation.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials synthesized under controlled atmosphere, temperature, pressure, and post-treatment conditions.
The magnitude of catalytic improvement may depend on synthesis parameters other than precursor ratio.
